Execution flow

Execution Flow

Explore

  1. Determine application's/system's password policy: Determine the password policies of the target application/system.

    2. Techniques
    Determine minimum and maximum allowed password lengths.
    Determine format of allowed passwords (whether they are required or allowed to contain numbers, special characters, etc.).
    Determine account lockout policy (a strict account lockout policy will prevent brute force attacks).

Exploit

  1. Brute force password: Given the finite space of possible passwords dictated by the password policy determined in the previous step, try all possible passwords for a known user ID until application/system grants access.

    2. Techniques
    Manually or automatically enter all possible passwords through the application/system's interface. In most systems, start with the shortest and simplest possible passwords, because most users tend to select such passwords if allowed to do so.
    Perform an offline dictionary attack or a rainbow table attack against a known password hash.

Attack description

This attack exploits target software that constructs SQL statements based on user input. An attacker crafts input strings so that when the target software constructs SQL statements based on the input, the resulting SQL statement performs actions other than those the application intended. SQL Injection results from failure of the application to appropriately validate input.

Execution flow

Execution Flow

Explore

  1. Assess application: The initial action taken by the attacker is to inventory the functionalities that the application exposes.

    2. Techniques
    Spider websites to gather all available links
    Intercept network communications with the application using tools like WireShark.

Experiment

  1. Identify user-controllable input vulnerable to injection: Identify which user-controllable inputs may be susceptible to injection attacks. For each input that the attacker believes may be vulnerable to SQL injection, attempt to insert characters that hold special significance in SQL (such as a single quote, a double quote, two hyphens, a parenthesis, etc.). The aim is to generate a SQL query that contains invalid syntax.

    2. Techniques
    Employ a web browser to input data through text fields or via HTTP GET parameters.
    Utilize a web application debugging tool like Tamper Data, TamperIE, WebScarab, etc. to alter HTTP POST parameters, hidden fields, non-freeform fields, etc.
    Apply network-level packet injection tools such as netcat to input data
    Employ a modified client (altered through reverse engineering) to input data.

  2. Investigate SQL Injection vulnerabilities: Once a specific input is confirmed to be susceptible to SQL Injection, theorize the structure of the underlying query. Iteratively attempt to add logic to this query to retrieve information from the database or to modify or delete database information.

    3. Techniques
    Reference public resources like the "SQL Injection Cheat Sheet" located at http://ferruh.mavituna.com/makale/sql-injection-cheatsheet/, and test various methods for appending logic to SQL queries.
    Incorporate logic into the query and utilize detailed error messages from the server to troubleshoot the query. For instance, if including a single quote in a query generates an error message, attempt: "' OR 1=1; --", or another syntactically valid completion of a hypothesized query. Refine the query iteratively.
    Implement "Blind SQL Injection" techniques to gather information regarding the database schema.
    Should the objective be a denial of service attack, experiment with stacked queries. This approach may not function on all platforms (notably, it is ineffective on Oracle or MySQL). Example inputs may include: "'; DROP TABLE SYSOBJECTS; --" and "'); DROP TABLE SYSOBJECTS; --". These specific queries are likely to fail due to the general protection of the SYSOBJECTS table.

Exploit

  1. Leverage SQL Injection vulnerability: After enhancing and appending various logic to SQL queries, formulate and execute the underlying SQL query intended for attacking the target system. The objective is to reveal, modify, and/or delete data within the database, employing the insights gained from the previous phase. This may involve crafting and executing several SQL queries if the aim is to conduct a denial of service attack.

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** ARP Cache Poisoning

Threat actors can manipulate Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) caches to place themselves in the communication path between multiple networked devices. This tactic can facilitate subsequent actions such as [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040) or [Transmitted Data Manipulation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1565/002).

The ARP protocol functions to map IPv4 addresses to link layer addresses, including media access control (MAC) addresses. Devices on a local network segment interact using link layer addresses. If a device lacks the link layer address for another device, it may broadcast an ARP request within the local network to resolve the IP address to a MAC address. The device corresponding to the specified IP address will respond directly with its MAC address. The device that initiated the ARP request will then utilize and retain that information within its ARP cache.

An adversary might wait passively for an ARP request to corrupt the ARP cache of the requesting device. By replying with their MAC address, the adversary misleads the victim into believing they are in communication with the correct networked device. To successfully poison the ARP cache, the adversary's reply must occur more quickly than that of the legitimate IP address owner. Additionally, adversaries may issue a gratuitous ARP reply that maliciously claims control of a specific IP address to all devices within the local network segment.

The ARP protocol lacks statefulness and does not incorporate authentication. Consequently, devices may incorrectly add or update the MAC address corresponding to an IP address in their ARP cache.

Threat actors may employ ARP cache poisoning as a strategy to intercept network traffic. This action can be used to gather and/or transmit sensitive information such as credentials, particularly those sent over insecure, unencrypted protocols.

Attack description

An attack of this type exploits a system's configuration that allows an adversary to either directly access an executable file, for example through shell access; or in a possible worst case allows an adversary to upload a file and then execute it. Web servers, ftp servers, and message oriented middleware systems which have many integration points are particularly vulnerable, because both the programmers and the administrators must be in synch regarding the interfaces and the correct privileges for each interface.

ATT&CK adversary context **Technique:** Network Service Discovery Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of services running on remote hosts and local network infrastructure devices, including those that may be vulnerable to remote software exploitation. Common methods to acquire this information include port, vulnerability, and/or wordlist scans using tools that are brought onto a system.(Citation: CISA AR21-126A FIVEHANDS May 2021) Within cloud environments, adversaries may attempt to discover services running on other cloud hosts. Additionally, if the cloud environment is connected to a on-premises environment, adversaries may be able to identify services running on non-cloud systems as well. Within macOS environments, adversaries may use the native Bonjour application to discover services running on other macOS hosts within a network. The Bonjour mDNSResponder daemon automatically registers and advertises a host’s registered services on the network. For example, adversaries can use a mDNS query (such as dns-sd -B _ssh._tcp .) to find other systems broadcasting the ssh service.(Citation: apple doco bonjour description)(Citation: macOS APT Activity Bradley)

**Technique:** Application Exhaustion Flood

Threat actors can exploit resource-heavy functionalities within applications to create a denial of service (DoS), thereby obstructing access to those applications. For instance, certain features in web applications can demand significant resources. Continuous requests to these features could potentially deplete system resources, resulting in limited access to the application or the server itself. (Citation: Arbor AnnualDoSreport Jan 2018)

Attack description

A malicious actor transmits a harmful response containing an "NXDOMAIN" ("No such domain") code or a DNS A record to a target's route inquiry prior to a legitimate resolver doing so. This method necessitates an On-path or In-path device capable of monitoring and replying to the target's DNS queries. Unlike BGP Tampering, this attack specifically responds to the requests issued by the target rather than contaminating the routing infrastructure utilized by the target.

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Exploit Public-Facing Application

Adversaries might seek to leverage vulnerabilities in an Internet-facing host or system to gain initial access to a network. These vulnerabilities can stem from software bugs, transient glitches, or misconfigurations within the system.

Applications that are exploited are frequently websites or web servers, but they can also encompass databases (such as SQL), standard services (including SMB or SSH), management protocols for network devices (like SNMP and Smart Install), and any other systems with Internet-accessible open ports. (Citation: NVD CVE-2016-6662)(Citation: CIS Multiple SMB Vulnerabilities)(Citation: US-CERT TA18-106A Network Infrastructure Devices 2018)(Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)(Citation: NVD CVE-2014-7169) In the case of ESXi infrastructure, adversaries might take advantage of exposed OpenSLP services or alternatively target exposed VMware vCenter servers. (Citation: Recorded Future ESXiArgs Ransomware 2023)(Citation: Ars Technica VMWare Code Execution Vulnerability 2021) Depending on the specific flaw being exploited, this could also involve [Exploitation for Stealth](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1211) or [Exploitation for Client Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1203).

When an application is hosted on cloud infrastructure or is containerized, exploiting it can result in the compromise of the underlying instance or container. This can create a pathway for an adversary to access cloud or container APIs (e.g., through the [Cloud Instance Metadata API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/005)), exploit container host access via [Escape to Host](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1611), or exploit weak identity and access management protocols.

Additionally, adversaries may target edge network infrastructure and associated appliances, specifically focusing on devices that lack robust host-based defenses. (Citation: Mandiant Fortinet Zero Day)(Citation: Wired Russia Cyberwar)

For websites and databases, the most prevalent web-based vulnerabilities are highlighted by the OWASP top 10 and CWE top 25. (Citation: OWASP Top 10)(Citation: CWE top 25)

Execution Flow

Execution Flow

Explore

  1. Identify Entry Point: The attacker begins by selecting a system to target and seeks an entry point that will enable the installation of the malicious software. This may involve a system with which they are already familiar, providing insights into its software and environment.

    2. Techniques
    Utilize a JTAGulator to find exposed JTAG and UART interfaces in smaller embedded devices.
    Locate exposed USB ports that could facilitate the loading of software.

  2. Identify Supply Chain Vulnerability: The attacker outlines the supply chain associated with the target system. They search for opportunities to physically access the system after it has been manufactured but prior to its deployment to the target.

    3. Techniques
    Acquire a system and monitor the shipment process it undergoes.
    Pinpoint potential warehouses where systems are stored post-manufacturing.

Experiment

  1. Evaluate Malicious Software: Prior to executing the attack in a live environment, an attacker will assess the attack on a system they have acquired to verify that the intended outcome will be achieved.

    2. Techniques
    Develop malicious software that provides the attacker with a backdoor into the system once it is deployed to the target.
    Acquire pre-existing malicious software that simply needs to be integrated into the system.

Exploit

  1. Insert Software into the Supply Chain: By leveraging the vulnerability identified in the supply chain during the exploration phase, the attacker embeds the malicious software into the system. This action grants the attacker unintended access to systems when they arrive at the target location, potentially leading to various subsequent attacks.

Requirements

The configuration of the system must permit an attacker to gain direct access to executable files or to upload files for execution. This indicates that any access control mechanism intended to regulate interactions between the subject and the object is misconfigured or operates under the assumption of a safe environment.

Requirements

The client software being targeted must support scripting interactions from remote sources, like a Web Browser with JavaScript capability.

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Brute Force

Adversaries might employ brute force methods to access accounts when the passwords are not known or when password hashes have been acquired. (Citation: TrendMicro Pawn Storm Dec 2020) In the absence of the password for one or more accounts, an adversary could methodically guess the password by employing a repetitive or iterative approach. (Citation: Dragos Crashoverride 2018) The process of brute forcing passwords can occur either through interaction with a service that verifies the validity of those credentials or offline against previously obtained credential data, like password hashes.

Credential brute forcing can occur at different stages during a breach. For instance, adversaries might attempt to brute force access to [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) within a compromised environment, using information gathered from other post-compromise activities such as [OS Credential Dumping](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003), [Account Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1087), or [Password Policy Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1201). Additionally, adversaries may integrate brute forcing efforts with activities like [External Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1133) as part of Initial Access.

Should an adversary successfully guess the correct password but be unable to log into a compromised account due to location-based conditional access policies, they might alter their infrastructure to align with the victim's location, thus circumventing those policies. (Citation: ReliaQuest Health Care Social Engineering Campaign 2024)

Execution flow

Execution Flow

Explore

  1. Examine the application for user-controllable inputs: An attacker utilizes a browser or an automated tool to navigate all public links and actions on a website. They compile a list of all links, forms, accessed resources, and other potential entry points for the web application.

    2. Techniques
    Employ a spidering tool to traverse and document all links and analyze the web pages to identify entry points. Pay special attention to any links that contain parameters in the URL.
    Utilize a proxy tool to log all links accessed during a manual exploration of the web application.
    Manually investigate the website using a browser and examine its structure. Various browser plugins are available to assist with the analysis or automate the discovery process.

Experiment

  1. Test identified potential entry points for XSS vulnerabilities: The attacker leverages the entry points collected in the "Explore" phase as a target list, injecting various common script payloads to ascertain whether an entry point represents a vulnerability and to gauge the extent of exploitability.

    2. Techniques
    Use a set of XSS probe strings to inject scripts into parameters of known URLs. If feasible, the probe strings should include a unique identifier.
    Employ a proxy tool to document the outcomes of manual XSS probe inputs on known URLs.
    Utilize a list of XSS probe strings to insert scripts into UI entry fields. If possible, the probe strings should contain a unique identifier.
    Use a list of XSS probe strings to inject scripts into resources utilized by the application. If feasible, the probe strings should include a unique identifier.

Exploit

  1. Acquire session IDs, credentials, page content, etc.: Upon successfully exploiting the vulnerability, the attacker may choose to steal user credentials for reuse or future analysis.

    2. Techniques
    Create malicious JavaScript that is injected via vectors identified during the Experiment Phase, which is then executed by the victim's browser to send document information to the attacker.
    Produce malicious JavaScript injected through vectors identified during the Experiment Phase that receives commands from an attacker's server, prompting the browser to execute the corresponding actions.

  2. Forced browsing: When the attacker targets the current application or another one (via CSRF vulnerabilities), the user unwittingly performs the attacks. These attacks primarily exploit application logic flaws, but they can also facilitate widespread attacks against a specific website on the user's current network (whether Internet or not).

    3. Techniques
    Create malicious JavaScript injected through vectors identified during the Experiment Phase that is executed by the victim's browser to perform actions on the same website.
    Develop malicious JavaScript injected via vectors identified during the Experiment Phase that receives commands from an attacker's server, causing the browser to issue requests to other websites (specifically those with CSRF vulnerabilities).

  3. Content spoofing

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Brute Force

Adversaries may use brute force techniques to gain access to accounts when passwords are unknown or when password hashes are obtained.(Citation: TrendMicro Pawn Storm Dec 2020) Without knowledge of the password for an account or set of accounts, an adversary may systematically guess the password using a repetitive or iterative mechanism.(Citation: Dragos Crashoverride 2018) Brute forcing passwords can take place via interaction with a service that will check the validity of those credentials or offline against previously acquired credential data, such as password hashes.

Brute forcing credentials may take place at various points during a breach. For example, adversaries may attempt to brute force access to [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) within a victim environment leveraging knowledge gathered from other post-compromise behaviors such as [OS Credential Dumping](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003), [Account Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1087), or [Password Policy Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1201). Adversaries may also combine brute forcing activity with behaviors such as [External Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1133) as part of Initial Access. 

If an adversary guesses the correct password but fails to login to a compromised account due to location-based conditional access policies, they may change their infrastructure until they match the victim’s location and therefore bypass those policies.(Citation: ReliaQuest Health Care Social Engineering Campaign 2024)

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Direct Network Flood

Adversaries may seek to achieve a denial of service (DoS) by sending a substantial amount of network traffic directly to a target. This DoS attack can diminish both the availability and functionality of the affected system(s) and network. [Direct Network Flood](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1498/001) refers to instances where one or more systems transmit a high volume of network packets aimed at the network of the targeted service. Nearly any network protocol can be utilized for such flooding. Although stateless protocols like UDP or ICMP are frequently employed, stateful protocols such as TCP can also be applicable.

Network flooding attacks are often executed using botnets that target various networks and services. Large-scale botnets can produce a considerable amount of traffic from devices distributed across the global Internet. Adversaries may either develop and manage their own botnet infrastructure or lease time on an existing botnet to carry out an attack. In some severe cases of distributed DoS (DDoS), the number of systems involved in generating the flood is so high that each one only needs to emit a minimal amount of traffic to create sufficient volume to overwhelm the target network. In these scenarios, it becomes extremely challenging to differentiate between DDoS traffic and that of legitimate clients. Some of the most notable DDoS flooding attacks have utilized botnets, including the series of incidents in 2012 that targeted prominent US banks. (Citation: USNYAG IranianBotnet March 2016)

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Scheduled Task/Job

Adversaries might exploit the functionality of task scheduling to enable initial or repeated execution of malicious code. All major operating systems provide utilities that allow the scheduling of programs or scripts to run at a designated date and time. It is also feasible to schedule a task on a remote system, given that the necessary authentication requirements are satisfied (for example, RPC and file and printer sharing in Windows environments). Generally, scheduling tasks on a remote system may necessitate membership in an administrative or similarly privileged group on that remote system. (Citation: TechNet Task Scheduler Security)

Adversaries may leverage task scheduling to run programs during system startup or on a regular schedule for persistence purposes. These mechanisms can also be exploited to initiate a process under the context of a specified account (such as one endowed with elevated permissions/privileges). In a manner akin to [System Binary Proxy Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218), adversaries have similarly exploited task scheduling to potentially disguise one-time execution as part of a trusted system process. (Citation: ProofPoint Serpent)

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Exploit Public-Facing Application

Adversaries may attempt to exploit a weakness in an Internet-facing host or system to initially access a network. The weakness in the system can be a software bug, a temporary glitch, or a misconfiguration.

Exploited applications are often websites/web servers, but can also include databases (like SQL), standard services (like SMB or SSH), network device administration and management protocols (like SNMP and Smart Install), and any other system with Internet-accessible open sockets.(Citation: NVD CVE-2016-6662)(Citation: CIS Multiple SMB Vulnerabilities)(Citation: US-CERT TA18-106A Network Infrastructure Devices 2018)(Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)(Citation: NVD CVE-2014-7169) On ESXi infrastructure, adversaries may exploit exposed OpenSLP services; they may alternatively exploit exposed VMware vCenter servers.(Citation: Recorded Future ESXiArgs Ransomware 2023)(Citation: Ars Technica VMWare Code Execution Vulnerability 2021) Depending on the flaw being exploited, this may also involve [Exploitation for Stealth](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1211) or [Exploitation for Client Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1203).

If an application is hosted on cloud-based infrastructure and/or is containerized, then exploiting it may lead to compromise of the underlying instance or container. This can allow an adversary a path to access the cloud or container APIs (e.g., via the [Cloud Instance Metadata API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/005)), exploit container host access via [Escape to Host](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1611), or take advantage of weak identity and access management policies.

Adversaries may also exploit edge network infrastructure and related appliances, specifically targeting devices that do not support robust host-based defenses.(Citation: Mandiant Fortinet Zero Day)(Citation: Wired Russia Cyberwar)

For websites and databases, the OWASP top 10 and CWE top 25 highlight the most common web-based vulnerabilities.(Citation: OWASP Top 10)(Citation: CWE top 25)
